title: A Palace in Time
hook: Heschel described Shabbat as a sanctuary built not of stone but of time
carry: shabbat is a palace built in time
tomorrow: who's really doing the searching, you or God?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Heschel on a Berlin street, catching the evening prayer late, and learning that awe comes before faith. Wonder first. Today, the same teacher solves a puzzle in the Torah's first pages.

Saba David's house is sold. On the phone he asked Noa a quiet question: where will we do Friday dinners now? Hold that, because here's the puzzle. Heschel read the opening chapters of Genesis looking for the first thing the Torah calls holy. You'd guess a mountain, a temple, an altar, a sacred tree. It's none of those. It's a day. "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Why would the very first holy thing be something you can't stand on, build, or sell?
screen: `WHERE WILL WE DO FRIDAYS NOW?` → `THE FIRST THING CALLED HOLY...` → `...IS A DAY.`

segments.voice: Heschel's answer, in his small book The Sabbath, is that Judaism is a religion of time. A technical civilization, he says, pours its effort into space: what we can own, build and point at. The Torah turns the eye somewhere else. Before any sanctuary of stone, it hallows a stretch of hours. He called Shabbat a palace in time, and he said the Sabbaths are Judaism's great cathedrals. That's the fact to repeat tonight: the Torah's first holy thing, in Heschel's reading, is the seventh day. And here's what solves Noa's puzzle. A palace in time can't be sold with a house. It doesn't get left behind in a move. Wherever the candles are lit and the week is set down, the palace is standing, in a new apartment or a dorm room or a kitchen far from home. Heschel doesn't say places don't matter. Jewish life has synagogues, homes, a holy city. But time comes first in the Torah's own order, and time travels. So does a table, as long as someone keeps the hour.
screen: `A RELIGION OF TIME.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · `THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.` · `TIME TRAVELS WITH YOU.` · then, large: `HOLINESS BUILT IN TIME.`

segments.voice: Choose one hour this week to set apart. Decide what stays out of it, a phone or errands, and what goes in: a meal, a walk, a person. Say the day and the hour quietly to yourself, as if you were laying its first stone.
screen: `ONE HOUR, SET APART.` · `WHAT STAYS OUT.` · `WHAT GOES IN.`

segments.voice: Holiness built in time: Heschel's reading of Shabbat as a sanctuary made of hours, not stone, which goes wherever its keepers go.
Keep this one: shabbat is a palace built in time. A house can be sold; the seventh day can't be.

howItsDone: Shabbat runs from sunset Friday to nightfall Saturday; Jews who keep it mark its start with candles and a blessing over wine and bread, at home or wherever they are.
